original_value: Optical sensors have shown high capabilities to improve the detection and monitoring of plant disease development. This study was designed to compare the feasibility of different sensors to characterize Fusarium head blight (FHB) caused by Fusarium graminearum and Fusarium culmorum. Under controlled conditions, time-series measurements were performed with infrared thermography (IRT), chlorophyll fluorescence imaging (CFI), and hyperspectral imaging (HSI) starting 3 days after inoculation (dai). IRT allowed the visualization of temperature differences within the infected spikelets beginning 5 dai. At the same time, a disorder of the photosynthetic activity was confirmed by CFI via maximal fluorescence yields of spikelets (Fm) 5 dai. Pigment-specific simple ratio PSSRa and PSSRb derived from HSI allowed discrimination between Fusarium-infected and non-inoculated spikelets 3 dai. This effect on assimilation started earlier and was more pronounced with F. graminearum. Except the maximum temperature difference (MTD), all parameters derived from different sensors were significantly correlated with each other and with disease severity (DS). A support vector machine (SVM) classification of parameters derived from IRT, CFI, or HSI allowed the differentiation between non-inoculated and infected spikelets 3 dai with an accuracy of 78, 56 and 78%, respectively. Combining the IRT-HSI or CFI-HSI parameters improved the accuracy to 89% 30 dai.

result.paraphrase: Optical sensors have demonstrated strong potential for improving detection and monitoring of plant disease progression. This study compared the ability of different sensors to characterize Fusarium head blight (FHB) caused by Fusarium graminearum and Fusarium culmorum. Under controlled conditions, time-series data were collected with infrared thermography (IRT), chlorophyll fluorescence imaging (CFI), and hyperspectral imaging (HSI) beginning 3 days after inoculation (dai). IRT revealed temperature differences within infected spikelets starting at 5 dai. At the same time, CFI confirmed reduced photosynthetic activity through maximal fluorescence yields of spikelets (Fm) at 5 dai. Pigment-specific simple ratio PSSRa and PSSRb from HSI made it possible to distinguish Fusarium-infected from non-inoculated spikelets at 3 dai. This assimilation effect appeared earlier and was more pronounced with F. graminearum. With the exception of the maximum temperature difference (MTD), all parameters from the different sensors were significantly correlated with one another and with disease severity (DS). Support vector machine (SVM) classification of parameters from IRT, CFI, or HSI differentiated non-inoculated from infected spikelets at 3 dai with accuracies of 78, 56, and 78%, respectively. Combining IRT-HSI or CFI-HSI parameters raised accuracy to 89% at 30 dai.
